newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Cetes still seen a good investment bet.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Cetes still seen a good investment bet.

text.p: Mexico's primary treasury bill rates could fall a little more after their seven-week slide, but are still a good bet, particularly for dollar-based investors looking for high yields, analysts said on Thursday.
They said both domestic and foreign investors in Cetes could benefit by aiming at longer-term denominations, especially with inflation seen on a downward trend from the heights of the last two years.
There may be a little more room for interest rates to fall before hitting a floor, they said.
"I think we are getting to close to what is the bottom for interest rates. If we are not at the bottom we are close to the bottom," said ING Barings Mexico City economist Sergio Martin.

He forecasts that at most the shorter-term government paper could fall by another 100 basis points. With real returns closer to six or seven percent, the longer-term Cetes could fall a bit more, from 100 to 200 basis points, he said.
Bear Stearns & Co. on Thursday recommended buying three, six and 12 month Cetes.
The company expects the peso to end the year at 8.5 per dollar, which implies returns of about 13 percent for the Cetes.
"Thirteen percent is better than what you are getting in most dollar-denominated assets from the UMS (United Mexican States)," said Bear Stearns debt analyst Tulio Vera.
"Obviously it is not as good as it was a few weeks or months go, but it is becoming harder and harder to find comparable yields in the emerging markets," he said.
The bellwether one-month Cetes rate hit 29.89 percent in mid-November last year during another spell of peso volatility.
The one-month rate then fell to 27.02 percent in early December, rose a touch to 27.37 percent on December 17 before sliding to 21.45 percent at Banco de Mexico's primary auction this week.
That, of course, is way down from the sky-high rates seen during 1995 after the peso crashed. For example, during April 1995 the 28-day treasury bill rate yielded an average 74.84 percent.
With inflation on a downward trend, real returns on the treasury bills could improve as the year progresses, analysts said.
The main question on dollar-based returns, however, is how stable the peso will remain.

Analysts expect some period of volatility in the exchange rate before key mid-term elections in July this year, but opinions vary as to when that expected volatility will start to affect financial markets.
The political noise and an exchange rate adjustment could be followed by both interest rate and exchange rate volatility, they said.
Since the central bank has aimed to smooth volatility in the exchange rate, this could lead to another period of tighter monetary conditions, in this case higher interest rates, economists said.

"The central bank will try not to let it (a depreciation of the peso) go too far and... we could see interest rates going to 25 or 27 percent," said ING Baring's Martin, forecasting peso instability near the end of February.

"But then they will start to go down again as people see the exchange rate is stable again unless political circumstances are so special that people will be afraid of what will happen to the exchange rate," he said.
The peso has remained strong recently on strong foreign inflows of capital.

Morgan Stanley said in a recent report that one concern in Mexico is how to keep the peso from strengthening given the foreign flows "amid concerns that the government may prefer a strong currency, low interest rate environment in the run up to the election."
